full_judgment:
5. Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the preemptee opposite parties on the other hand submits that sufficiency or insufficiency of the evidence is a matter to be looked into by the court of facts and in the instant case both the courts below on due consideration of the evidence and materials on record arrived at a concurrent finding of fact that the deed in question is not a deed of sale but a deed of release. The learned Advocate further submits that in the instant case there is no necessity of examining any attesting witness or the scribe of the deed in question in support of their case by the pre-emptee opposite parties inasmuch as attesting witnesses only prove the execution of the documents and they are not competent to prove the contents of the same and in the instant case the positive case of the pre-emptee opposite parties is that the pre-emptor in collusion with the executants of the deeds managed to write the deed as a deed of sale instead of ''Nadabi'' deed. The learned Advocate further submits that there is no bar in relying on the single testimony of a witness if it appears to be true to the Court and in the instant case both the courts below relying on the testimony of DW 3 arrived at a finding that no consideration was passed in respect of the deed dated 20-12-80 and on this is essentially a question of fact and relying on the testimony of DW 3 the learned courts below arrived at such a finding and it is a clean finding of fact which cannot be reopened before this Court unless it can be shown that the finding is based on no evidence at all but admittedly there is some evidence for the court to arrive at such finding. So, sufficiency or insufficiency of evidence cannot be the ground for interference by this Court with the impugned judgment and order. The learned Advocate then submits that the main grievance of the pre-emptor petitioner is that both the courts below relying on extraneous evidence arrived at a finding that the deed in question is not a deed of sale, rather it is a deed of release and that contravenes the provisions of section 92 of the Evidence Act. The learned Advocate further submits that this submission made by Mr. Ruhul Amin, the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor, petitioner is not tenable in law inasmuch as section 92 of the Evidence Act prohibits a party to the agreement to lead evidence to add, vary or subtract from the terms of written instrument but in the instant case it is not a question of addition, varying or subtracting which will in the terms of the agreement rather in the instant case the question is what is the nature and character of the deed in question. The pre-emptor petitioner claimed the deed to be a deed of sale whereas the pre-emptee opposite parties claimed that it is a deed of release and in such circumstances the courts were competent to look into the nature and character of the deed in question and perfectly entitled to decide the nature and character of the documents and in support of his contention the learned Advocate relies on the following decisions, namely, 12 DLR 149, 19 DLR 17 and 654, 1988 BLD 33, 1986 BLD 85, AIR 1950 (SC) 15, AIR 1958 (SC) 448 and 1955 (Bombay) 320. 

 10. Section 92 presupposes the validity of the transaction evidenced by the document. If its validity is impeached, the court is not bound by what has been described as the paper expression of the parties, and is not precluded from entering into the real nature of the transaction between them. Section 92 does not preclude a party from showing that the writing was not really the contract between the parties, but was only a fictitious or colourable device which cloaked something else. Oral evidence is admissible to show that an agreement was only a sham or nominal transaction and was not intended to be acted upon or to show that a written agreement for the conveyance of property was only a fictitious sale to avoid execution proceedings against the property. In the case reported in AIR 1936 (PC) 70, the Privy Council observed. "section 92 only includes oral evidence to vary the terms of the written contract and has no reference to the question whether the parties had agreed to contract on the terms set forth in the document." Thus there is a material difference between an attempt to show that the terms of a contract were different from those recorded in a deed, and an attempt to show that the contract as mentioned in the deed was not the real contract between the parties but it was something different. It is the former that is hit by section 91 but the latter is not so hit. In the case reported in AIR 1931 (Orissa) 177, it has been held that where a husband admits that he executed a gift in favour of his wife, but alleges that he had no intention of giving away the property, oral evidence in proof of such defence is admissible. From the case reported in 1986 BLD 85, it appears that in that case an application for pre-emption was resisted by the pre-emptee on the ground that the deed in question though registered as a deed of sale but, in fact, it was a deed of exchange. It was contended on behalf of the pre-emptor that oral evidence is not admissible to prove that a document is not what it purports to be. But the court relying on the decisions reported in AIR 1958 (SC) 448 held that section 92 of the Evidence Act is not a bar to leading of oral evidence to prove that the document in question is not a sale deed but an exchange deed and I do not find any reason why this will not apply to the instant case although the deed is registered as a sale deed but it is contended by the pre-emptee opposite parties that it is, in fact, a deed of release and both the courts below concurrently found that the deed in question is in fact a deed of release and in arriving in that concurrent finding, in my opinion, the courts below did not commit any error of law. Similarly in the case reported in 1988 BLD 33 it has been held that admission of oral evidence of the acts and conducts of the parties in determining the true nature of the transaction does not infringe provision of section 92 of the Evidence Act. It can be shown by oral evidence that though a document in particular form was executed in fact it is different from what it appears to be. When a document is meant merely on an informal memorandum of transaction and not as a document embodying disposition of property, oral evidence is not excluded. Similarly, in the case reported in 19 DLR 17 it has been held that operation of section 92 of the Evidence Act is confined to the parties to an instrument and this decision is in line with the decision reported in AIR 1958 (SC) 448, wherein their Lordships of the Supreme Court of India held that section 92 applies only in case of parties to the contract and similar is the view reflected in the decision reported in PLD 1960 (Lohore) 231. It has further been held in the 19 DLR's case that the parol evidence of surrounding circumstances along with the contents of the relevant documents may be taken into consideration for the purpose of construing a document and holding whether the evidence so justified with the same, though couched in a particular form is really different. Furthermore, section 92 merely prescribes a rule of evidence. It does not fetter the Court's power to arrieve at the true meaning and effect of a transaction in the light of the surrounding circumstances. Yet there is another decision which contradicted in the instance case, that is, the case reported in 12 DLR 149 wherein it has been held that a recital in the document showing that the donor has given delivery of possession of the hiba land is no doubt binding on him and also on the persons claiming through him. But from that it does not necessarily follow that they are not entitled to disprove the recital. Oral evidence which goes to vary the terms of the contract may not be admitted into evidence between the parties. But if it is not related to any terms or intend to vary or add to or subtract from its terms, there is no bar of adducing oral evidence to prove matters other than those specifically mentioned in section 92 of the Evidence Act. 

 12. In the case reported in AIR 1962 (Madras) 360 it has been held that there is material difference between an attempt to show that the terms of the contract were different from those recorded in a deed and an attempt to show that the contract as mentioned in the deed was not the real contract between the parties but it was something different. It is the former that is hit by section 91 of the Evidence Act but the latter is not so hit. Thus where the contention of the plaintiff is that the actual contract itself was different and that for certain reasons it was made to appear in the document that it was a rectification deed, section 91 does not preclude the plaintiff from proving that the real contract was different from what is found in the deed. Thus, here the contention of the plaintiff is that the actual contract itself was different, and that for certain reasons it was made to appear in the document that it was a rectification deed, section 91 does not preclude the plaintiff from proving that the real contract was different from what is found in the deed. Similarly in the case reported in AIR 1955 (Bombay) 320 it has been held that there is no difficulty in spite of sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act in leading evidence to show, notwithstanding the recital of payment of consideration in a document, that it was actually not paid. In the case reported in AIR 1958 (50.15, it has been held that extrinsic evidence to determine the effect of an instrument is permissible where there remains a doubt as to its true meaning. Similarly, in the case reported in AIR 1938 (Nagpur) 335 it has been held that all that section 92, Evidence Act excludes is oral evidence to contradict, vary, add to, or subtract from terms of a contract which has been reduced to writing. It does not preclude a party from showing that the writing was not really the contract between the parties but was only a fictitious or colourable device which cloaked something else. In the case reported in 95 Indian Cases 512 it has been held that where a person who has executed a document seeks to show that the document is a mere sham deed and represents nothing he is not seeking to vary or contradict any of the terms of the document and oral evidence is admissible to prove that there was no such agreement between the parties as is represented by the document.
